title: Business Registration & Compliance for Product Makers: NAFDAC, SON and Safe Production
subtitle: Take a food, cosmetic or manufactured product from your workshop to a legally approved, traceable product that bigger buyers can stock.
description: A hands-on, advanced course for women who make products. You choose the right NAFDAC or SON route, build a vetting pack, prepare an inspection-ready production room, cost compliance into your price, and set up batch records, recalls and renewals that keep your products on the shelf.
outcomes: Decide whether your products fit NAFDAC's micro scale, small scale or regular route, or need SON MANCAP
Prepare a locked master formula, honest best-before date and a label with every required field
Set up a designated production room with one-way flow, hygiene records and pest control
Calculate compliance cost per unit and plan batch capacity for bigger orders
Run batch numbering, distribution records and a recall when something goes wrong
Keep a compliance calendar and a dated 90-day plan to stay approved
audience: Women who already make and sell food, cosmetic, household or other manufactured products and are ready to get them formally approved and into bigger markets.
tools: A smartphone with internet and a camera
Your CAC certificate or registration details
A kitchen scale that weighs in grams
A notebook or a spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets
A folder for your compliance file
Access to the NAFDAC e-registration portal and your nearest SON state office

modules.title: Foundations: Choosing Your Product's Approval Route
modules.overview: Before you fill any form, you need to know which NAFDAC route your product fits, what must be ready before you apply, and who in your business owns compliance. This module turns those three questions into decisions you can write down.

lessons.title: Micro scale, small scale or full registration: finding your product's NAFDAC route
objectives: Check whether your product is allowed under NAFDAC's micro and small scale scheme
Decide between the micro scale and small scale routes using staff, premises and product count
Choose which products to list first when you make more than five
Explain what a listing certificate is and how long it lasts

blocks.text: You already know that a packaged food or cosmetic needs NAFDAC approval before it is sold to the public. This lesson goes one level deeper: **which door do you knock on?** NAFDAC runs a special scheme for micro and small enterprises (MSMEs), with lower fees, simpler documents and an inspection you can book on a date that suits you. Many hands-on makers qualify, but not every product and not every workshop does. Getting the route right first saves you from paying for the wrong application.

blocks.name: woman-factory
blocks.alt: A woman worker in a small factory
blocks.caption: Your route depends on what you make, how many people make it and where they work.

blocks.text: Which products the MSME scheme accepts

NAFDAC's MSME page lists the product types it accepts. On the food side it names bread, packaged water, and cottage or kitchen-scale and micro-scale foods. It also states that some foods are **not** allowed under the micro scale route: meat and meat products (except dried), milk and dairy products, and fish and fish products (except dried). These are higher-risk foods because germs grow in them quickly.

On the cosmetic and household side, the page lists petroleum jelly, shea butter, oil-based hair cream, oils such as coconut oil, laundry detergents, starch, liquid air freshener and soaps. It says complex cosmetics, pressurised sprays and hand sanitisers do not qualify. If your product is not on these lists, it goes through NAFDAC's regular registration route, which asks for more documentation.

head: Your product
MSME scheme?
Why
rows: Chin-chin or cookies made in a dedicated room
Dry, lower-risk food named under the scheme
Shea butter is listed among allowed cosmetics
Bar soap and liquid laundry detergent
Soaps and laundry detergents are listed
Yoghurt or fresh fish pepper soup in packs
Dairy and fresh fish are excluded at micro scale
Face serum with several active ingredients
Complex cosmetics do not qualify; ask NAFDAC

blocks.text: Micro scale or small scale?

Inside the scheme there are two levels. NAFDAC describes a **micro scale facility** as a business with not more than five employees, in a building that can be purpose-built or adapted, with at least a **designated standard room that does not open directly to any source of contamination** (for example a toilet, a refuse dump or an open gutter). A **small scale facility** must have adequate space, capacity and equipment, and it is asked for more paperwork: written standard operating procedures (SOPs) for production, cleaning, hygiene, quality assurance and distribution, water analysis, and certificates of analysis for raw materials and finished products.

Two more rules shape your choice. Under micro scale, **not more than five products** can be registered. And what you receive at micro scale is a **listing certificate**, which NAFDAC states is valid for **two years**. Mark that date the day you collect it, because selling after expiry puts you back where you started.

blocks.title: Finding your route
items: Is the product type allowed?
Five or fewer staff?
Designated clean room ready?
Five or fewer products?
Apply micro scale
blocks.caption: If you answer no at any step, look at small scale or full registration instead.

blocks.title: Worked example: seven products, five slots
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Enugu has three workers and a spare room she has converted for production. She makes seven products: chin-chin, coconut candy, plantain chips, zobo concentrate, whipped shea butter, black soap and a liquid laundry detergent.
steps: She checks each product type against the MSME lists. All seven appear to fit allowed categories, so none is excluded by type.
She has three workers, within the five-employee limit for micro scale, and a dedicated room with no direct opening to a toilet or drain.

Seven products is more than the five allowed at micro scale, so she ranks them by monthly sales: chin-chin 300 packs, shea butter 120 jars, plantain chips 110 packs, black soap 90 bars, detergent 60 bottles, coconut candy 40 packs, zobo 25 bottles.
She lists the top five first. Together they are 680 of her 745 monthly units.
She works out the share: 680 divided by 745 is about 0.91, so 91 percent of her volume will be covered by the first applications.
blocks.result: Amaka applies at micro scale for five products covering about 91 percent of her sales, and pauses coconut candy and zobo for public sale until she can add them, possibly by moving up to small scale later.

blocks.title: A route is about the facility too
blocks.text: The same shea butter can qualify in one woman's workshop and fail in another's. If your only production space is the family kitchen that also opens onto the toilet passage, fix the room first. The route depends on where and how you make the product, not only on what it is.
When to go straight to small scale

items: You already employ more than five people in production, so you are beyond NAFDAC's micro scale facility description.
You want to list more than five products in the near future and do not want to apply twice.
You already work from a purpose-built space with enough room and equipment for larger batches.
You can write the SOPs (cleaning, hygiene, production, quality, distribution) and pay for water analysis and certificates of analysis.

blocks.text: Write your decision on one page: product names, the category each falls under, your staff count, a one-line description of your production room, and the route you have chosen. This page becomes the first sheet of your compliance file and the starting point for the rest of the course.

takeaways: The MSME scheme accepts named food and simple cosmetic or household products; high-risk foods and complex cosmetics are excluded at micro scale.
Micro scale means not more than five employees and at least one designated room not open to contamination.
Micro scale allows not more than five products, so rank yours by sales.
The micro scale listing certificate is valid for two years.

activity.title: Map your route
steps: List every product you make or plan to make.
Mark each one: allowed under MSME, excluded, or unsure (to ask NAFDAC).
Count your production staff and describe your production room in two lines.
If you have more than five products, rank them by monthly units and choose the first five.
Write your chosen route at the top of the page.
activity.evidence: A one-page route decision sheet with your ranked product list.

lessons.title: Building your vetting pack: locked formula, honest shelf life and a label that passes
objectives: Lock a written formula and process before you apply
Set a best-before date from your own storage checks instead of guessing
Prepare the vetting sample, three labels and the supporting certificates
Lay out every label field NAFDAC's MSME procedure asks for

blocks.text: NAFDAC's MSME procedure asks for a small set of items: evidence of CAC registration, a site use agreement where it applies, trademark documentation (optional at micro scale), **one vetting sample and three labels**, a fumigation certificate, food handler or medical fitness certificates for staff, and the payment receipt. Most delays come from the parts that only you can produce: a stable product and a correct label. This lesson is about those.

blocks.name: document-ready
blocks.alt: A woman holding a finished document beside a checklist
blocks.caption: A complete vetting pack means the inspector sees a product that is already settled.

blocks.text: Step 1: lock the formula

The sample NAFDAC tests must be the product you will sell. If you change the recipe after approval, you are selling something that was not assessed. Before you apply, write a **master formula**: every ingredient, its supplier, the exact quantity per batch in grams or millilitres, and the method in numbered steps with times and temperatures. Make at least three batches from this sheet and check that they come out the same.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a kitchen recipe into a master formula
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin makes whipped shea butter by feel: a scoop of shea, some coconut oil, a few drops of fragrance oil.
steps: She weighs one normal batch: 1,600 g shea butter, 300 g coconut oil, 80 g sweet almond oil and 20 g fragrance oil. Total 2,000 g.
She converts to percentages: 1,600 divided by 2,000 is 80 percent shea; coconut 15 percent; almond 4 percent; fragrance 1 percent. The four add up to 100 percent.
She writes the method: melt shea and oils at low heat, cool until just setting, whip 8 minutes, fill 200 g jars.
From 2,000 g she fills 10 jars of 200 g each.
She makes three batches from the sheet. All three fill 10 jars, smell the same and set the same.
blocks.result: Rukayat now has a master formula she can scale (for 4,000 g, double every weight) and a product that is the same every time, which is what the vetting sample must represent.

blocks.text: Step 2: set an honest best-before date

Do not copy another brand's shelf life. Keep **retained samples** from each trial batch, sealed in the real pack, in the conditions a buyer would use: a shelf at room temperature, away from sun. Check them at fixed points, for example every two weeks, for smell, colour, texture, mould, rancidity or separation. Write each result down. Set your best-before date **shorter than the last check that was still fully good**. If you need longer life, a food or cosmetic testing laboratory can test for microbes and rancidity, and its report will strengthen your file.

blocks.title: Shelf-life check for a 12-week target
items: Week 0: seal samples
Week 2: first check
Week 6: mid check
Week 10: last good check
Set best-before at 8 weeks
blocks.caption: The date you print comes from what you observed, with a safety margin.

blocks.text: Step 3: design a label with every required field
The MSME procedure lists what the label must carry, in **English**. Lay your design out as a checklist so nothing is missing before you print the three labels.

head: Field
What to write
Common mistake
rows: The common name, for example 'Whipped Shea Body Butter'
Only a brand name with no product description
A code that links to your batch record
Clear dates, for example MFD 03/2026, BB 05/2026
Dates written by hand later, or missing
A space reserved until a number is issued
'Store in a cool dry place, close lid after use'
'Contains nut oil', 'Dispose of empty jar responsibly'
Missing when nut or other allergens are used

blocks.title: Allergens are a safety field, not decoration
blocks.text: Groundnut, sesame, wheat, egg, milk and tree nut oils such as almond can cause serious reactions in some people. If any is in your product, even in a small amount, name it clearly in the ingredients and in an allergy caution line.
Step 4: book the certificates that take time

items: **Fumigation certificate:** arrange pest control for the production premises by a pest control operator and keep the certificate.
**Medical fitness certificates:** NAFDAC lists sputum, stool, urine, Widal and Hepatitis B tests for food handlers. Book these for everyone who will touch the product.
**Site use agreement:** if you rent or use a relative's building, get a signed letter or tenancy showing you may use it for production.
**Trademark:** optional at micro scale, but start it if you plan to grow, because it protects your brand name.

blocks.text: Put all of these in one folder, paper or on your phone, and name each file clearly, for example '2026-03 fumigation certificate.pdf'. When the portal asks for uploads, you will not be searching.

takeaways: The vetting sample must be exactly the product you will sell, so lock the formula first.
Write recipes as weights and percentages that add up to 100 percent.
Set best-before dates from your own retained-sample checks, with a margin.
Use the MSME label field list, in English, and reserve space for the NAFDAC number.
Book fumigation and staff medical tests early because they take time.

activity.title: Assemble your vetting pack
steps: Weigh one batch of your lead product and write the master formula with percentages.
Seal three retained samples in the real pack and start a dated check sheet.
Draft your label and tick every field from the table in this lesson.
List the certificates you still need and the date you will book each one.
activity.evidence: Your master formula sheet, shelf-life check sheet and a photo of the draft label with all fields ticked.

lessons.title: Owning compliance as the producer: roles, touts and the real cost of shortcuts
objectives: Name a compliance lead and write clear duties for each person in production
Recognise the warning signs of fake numbers and paid shortcuts
Verify claims and report suspect products through official NAFDAC channels
Write your producer's non-negotiables

blocks.text: A NAFDAC number is not a sticker you buy. It is a promise that a named business, in a named place, makes a product the same safe way every time. If something goes wrong, the name and address on your label lead back to you. That is why the business owner, not the cousin who helps or the agent who 'knows people', has to own compliance.

blocks.name: team-collaboration
blocks.alt: A small team working together around a shared plan
blocks.caption: Clear roles mean every person knows which part of compliance is theirs.

blocks.text: Give compliance a name and a desk
In a small workshop, the owner is usually the **compliance lead**. If you have staff, write down who does what. A short role sheet on the wall works better than instructions given once and forgotten.

head: Role
Duties
Checked by
rows: Keeps the compliance file, books inspections and renewals, approves label changes
Follows the master formula, fills the batch record, keeps retained samples
Cleans the room to the schedule, records pest checks
Records which batch went to which buyer, logs complaints

blocks.title: Who carries compliance
items: Owner: final responsibility
Production lead: every batch
Every worker: daily hygiene
blocks.caption: Responsibility rests at the top, but daily habits at the base keep it real.

blocks.text: Responsibility also runs backwards to your suppliers. If you buy shea butter, palm kernel oil, flour or fragrance from a market trader, the trader's word is not proof of quality. Buy from sellers who give a receipt with their name, keep that receipt with the batch record, and check packed ingredients for a NAFDAC number and an expiry date. A cheap drum of oil with no label can ruin a batch, and the complaint will come to you, not to the trader.

Finally, give yourself one fixed hour each month as **compliance day**. Open the file, check that certificates are in date, read the last month of batch and cleaning records, and note anything to fix. Owners who protect that hour rarely get caught by surprise.
Shortcuts that cost more than they save
Pressure from buyers pushes some makers toward shortcuts. Here are the common ones, and why each one is dangerous for you and your customers.

items: **Borrowing another brand's number.** The number belongs to a different product and premises. If anything goes wrong, you have no defence.
**Inventing a number or printing 'NAFDAC approved'.** This is misleading and can lead to seizure of your stock and loss of the customers you worked hard to win.

**Paying someone who promises a number in a week.** NAFDAC's own procedure involves inspection and laboratory analysis, with a stated timeline of ninety working days. A promise that skips those steps is a warning sign.
**Approving one formula and selling another.** Swapping a cheaper oil or preservative after approval means the product on the shelf was never assessed.

blocks.title: How to protect yourself from agents
blocks.text: Apply through NAFDAC's e-registration portal (registration.nafdac.gov.ng) or a NAFDAC state office, and pay only against an official payment advice through Remita. Keep your own login. If someone asks for cash 'for the inspector', do not pay. NAFDAC lists 0800-1-NAFDAC (0800-1-623322) for complaints and 0700-1-NAFDAC for enquiries.

blocks.title: Worked example: a supermarket order and a tempting offer
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Ibadan makes coconut candy. A supermarket wants 200 packs a month but needs a NAFDAC number. A man at the market offers to 'arrange' a number for her in seven days for a fee.
steps: Funmi asks: will there be an inspection of my room and lab tests of my product? He says no. That alone tells her it is not a genuine registration.
She calculates what she risks: 200 packs at about ₦1,500 each (approximate) is ₦300,000 of monthly sales that could be seized, plus the supermarket relationship.
She tells the buyer honestly that her application is starting, and asks whether they can begin once her listing certificate arrives.
She submits on the portal, books her inspection for three weeks ahead, and sends the buyer a short update every month.
blocks.result: Funmi starts later than she hoped, but with a real number tied to her own premises, and a buyer who has seen her handle the process professionally.

blocks.text: Your producer's non-negotiables

items: We sell only products that match the approved formula and label.
We never print a number we were not issued, and never use another brand's number.
We record every batch and keep retained samples.
We stop selling a batch at once if there is a safety complaint, until we understand it.
We deal with NAFDAC directly, using our own login and official payments.

blocks.text: Print your non-negotiables and put them where your team works. When a busy week tempts someone to skip a step, the rule is already decided, so nobody has to argue about it.

takeaways: The owner carries final responsibility for compliance, even when others help.
Written roles with a named checker stop steps being skipped.
Any offer that skips inspection and lab testing is not a real registration.
Pay only against official payment advice and keep your own portal login.

activity.title: Write your compliance roles and rules
steps: Write a role sheet for everyone involved, even if it is just you and one helper.
Write five non-negotiables in your own words.
Save NAFDAC's enquiry and complaint numbers in your phone.
Print or display the sheet in your production room.
activity.evidence: A photo of your role sheet and non-negotiables displayed in your workspace.

quiz.q: Kemi makes fresh yoghurt with two helpers in a clean dedicated room. Which statement is correct?
options: She should apply as a cosmetic product
Milk and dairy products are excluded under the micro scale route, so she needs another route
She qualifies for micro scale because she has fewer than five staff
Yoghurt needs no NAFDAC approval if sold on WhatsApp
quiz.explain: NAFDAC's MSME page excludes milk and dairy products from the micro scale route, whatever the staff count.

quiz.q: Amaka makes seven eligible products at micro scale. What should she do?
options: List up to five, chosen by sales, and plan the rest for later or small scale
Register one product and use its number on all seven
Wait until she has ten products
Register all seven at once under micro scale
quiz.explain: Not more than five products can be registered under micro scale, and the number must never be shared across products.

quiz.q: A batch uses 1,200 g shea butter, 240 g coconut oil, 120 g almond oil and 40 g fragrance. What percentage is shea butter?
quiz.explain: Total is 1,600 g. 1,200 divided by 1,600 is 0.75, so 75 percent.

quiz.q: Her retained samples were fully good at week 10 and showed slight rancidity at week 12. What best-before should she print?
options: No date until NAFDAC sets one
Shorter than 10 weeks, for example 8 weeks
quiz.explain: Set the date shorter than the last fully good check to leave a safety margin.

quiz.q: Which label line is NOT acceptable before a NAFDAC number is issued?
options: Store in a cool, dry place
quiz.explain: Claiming approval before it is granted is misleading. Leave a reserved space for the number instead.

quiz.q: Someone offers to get Funmi a NAFDAC number in seven days with no inspection or lab test. What is the best response?
options: Use a friend's number until hers arrives
Print 'registration in progress' with a made-up number
Pay, because the supermarket is waiting
Decline, apply through the official portal and update the buyer honestly
quiz.explain: Genuine registration includes facility inspection and laboratory analysis. Shortcuts risk seizure and loss of customers.

modules.title: Systems: The Application, the Production Room and the Numbers
modules.overview: This module takes you through the NAFDAC e-registration process and inspection day, shows you how to set up a production room that passes good manufacturing and hygiene checks, and teaches you to build compliance costs into your unit price and batch plan.

lessons.title: From portal to certificate: the application and inspection day, stage by stage
objectives: Move through the six stages of NAFDAC's MSME procedure in order
Convert ninety working days into a realistic calendar plan
Prepare your room, records and people for the inspector's visit
Respond correctly if the inspection or laboratory result is not satisfactory

blocks.text: NAFDAC's MSME procedure has six stages: apply online (or get forms at a state office), submit the completed form with documents, book your facility inspection, have samples collected during the inspection and sent to the laboratory, get scheduled for approval once the good manufacturing practice (GMP) inspection and lab results are satisfactory, and collect your certificate. The stated timeline from the first stage to the last is **ninety working days**. This lesson is about doing each stage well, so your file does not stall.

blocks.name: inspection
blocks.alt: A person inspecting items with a magnifying glass
blocks.caption: Inspection day is where your room, records and product are checked together.

blocks.text: Stages 1 and 2: the portal and the payment

items: Create your account on NAFDAC's e-registration portal (registration.nafdac.gov.ng) with your business email and a phone number you control. Write the login in your compliance file.
Enter your company details exactly as they appear on your CAC certificate. A different spelling or address causes queries.
Add each product with its name, pack size and category, using the same wording as your label.
Upload clear scans or photos of each document. One document per file, named clearly.
NAFDAC issues a payment advice. Pay through Remita using that advice only, and keep the receipt, which is itself one of the required documents.

blocks.text: Stage 3: booking the inspection

The procedure lets you **choose a convenient date** for the facility inspection. Use that freedom wisely. Pick a date at least two weeks after your fumigation, when your medical certificates are already in hand, and on a day you are actually producing, so the inspector can see your process, not an empty room.

blocks.title: A 90 working day plan
items: Week 1: apply and pay
Weeks 2 to 4: prepare room
Week 5: inspection and samples
Weeks 6 to 15: lab and review
Week 18: collect certificate
blocks.caption: Ninety working days is about eighteen weeks, so plan around four months, not four weeks.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning around a trade fair
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Aba wants her liquid laundry detergent approved before a trade fair in early October. It is now late April.
steps: She converts the timeline: 90 working days divided by 5 working days a week is 18 weeks.
She adds two weeks of buffer for public holidays and queries, giving 20 weeks.
Counting 20 weeks from 1 May takes her to about mid-September.
She applies on 1 May, books fumigation for 6 May, staff medical tests for the same week, and picks an inspection date in the first week of June.
She sets a reminder to check the portal every Friday for queries.
blocks.result: Her plan finishes around mid-September with a few weeks to spare before the fair. If she had started in July, the timeline could not have fitted.

blocks.text: Stage 4: what the inspector looks at
The inspection checks good manufacturing practice and good hygiene practice. Prepare as if you were the inspector. Walk into your own room and look for the things below.

items: **The room:** a designated production room that does not open directly onto a toilet, refuse or drain; clean walls, floor and work surfaces; screened windows.
**Water:** a clean, reliable supply for production and handwashing, with soap and a clean towel or paper.
**People:** workers in clean aprons and hair covers, with their medical fitness certificates on file.
**Materials:** raw materials stored off the floor, labelled, with supplier receipts; finished goods kept apart.
**Records:** your master formula, batch records, cleaning log and fumigation certificate, ready to show.
**Product:** enough finished product from a normal batch for samples to be taken for the laboratory.

blocks.title: Keep a 'show file' on the table
blocks.text: Put every document the inspector may ask for in one folder in the order of the checklist above. Calm, quick answers show that your system is real.
Stages 5 and 6: results, queries and the certificate

Approval is scheduled only after satisfactory GMP and laboratory results. If the inspector notes problems, you may be asked to correct them. Treat every query as a task list: fix each item, take a dated photo or get a document as proof, and reply through the official channel. Do not argue, and do not change the product to pass a test unless you update the formula and label to match.

When you are notified, collect the certificate, then scan it and keep the original safe. Write the issue date and the expiry date (two years later for a micro scale listing) on the first page of your compliance file and in your phone calendar, with a reminder six months before expiry. Only now do you add the number to your label artwork and print stock.

takeaways: The MSME procedure has six stages, with a stated timeline of ninety working days.
Ninety working days is about eighteen weeks; add buffer for holidays and queries.
Book your inspection on a production day, after fumigation and medical tests are done.
Answer queries with proof of each fix, through official channels.
Print the number on labels only after you hold the certificate.

activity.title: Build your application calendar
steps: Write today's date and your target approval date.
Count back 20 weeks to find your latest safe application date.
Fill in dates for fumigation, medical tests, portal submission and inspection.
Walk through your room with the inspector checklist and list every gap.
activity.evidence: A dated application calendar and a gap list from your self-inspection.

lessons.title: Setting up a production room that passes GMP and hygiene checks
objectives: Arrange a room so materials move one way, from raw to finished
Set up handwashing, cleaning and pest control that an inspector can see working
Apply the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food in a small production space
Write a daily cleaning log your team actually fills

blocks.text: NAFDAC's description of a micro scale facility asks for a **designated standard room that is not open directly to any source of contamination**. The word designated matters: it is a room used for production, not a family kitchen that also feeds the household, stores schoolbags and dries clothes. You do not need a factory. You need a clean, controlled room and habits that keep it that way.

blocks.name: broom
blocks.caption: Cleaning that is scheduled and recorded is what makes a room inspection-ready.

blocks.text: One-way flow: raw in, finished out

Contamination happens when dirty and clean things cross. Arrange your room so that raw materials enter on one side, move through preparation and processing, and leave as packed product on the other side, without going backwards. Waste should leave by a route that does not pass the packing table.

blocks.title: Production room flow
items: Raw material store
Weighing and preparation
Processing or mixing
Cooling and filling
Labelling and packed storage
blocks.caption: Materials move in one direction so finished product never meets raw or waste.

blocks.title: Worked example: converting a spare room
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos has a spare room about 3 metres by 4 metres for chin-chin production. Its back door opens toward the compound toilet.
steps: She works out the floor area: 3 m times 4 m is 12 square metres, enough for one worktable, a gas burner area, a cooling rack and a packing table.
Because the back door faces the toilet, she seals it and uses only the front door, which opens to the corridor.
She places a raw material shelf by the door, mixing table next, the frying area under the window with a screened mesh, the cooling rack after it, and the packing table in the far corner.
She installs a handwashing point inside the door with a covered bucket and tap, liquid soap and paper towels.
She buys a pedal bin with a lid, puts shelves 15 cm off the floor, and paints the walls in washable paint.
blocks.result: Grace's room now matches a one-way flow, has no direct opening to the toilet, and has handwashing and storage an inspector can see.

blocks.text: WHO Five Keys to Safer Food, in your room

head: WHO key
What it looks like in a small production room
rows: Wash hands before work, after the toilet and after handling raw materials; clean surfaces before and after each batch
Separate tables, utensils and storage for raw and finished goods
Follow the time and temperature in your master formula every batch
Cool cooked food quickly and pack only when cool; do not leave cooked items open for hours
Use safe water and raw materials
Clean water for production and washing; buy raw materials from traceable suppliers and check dates

blocks.text: Hygiene habits the inspector expects

items: **People:** clean apron, hair cover, short clean nails, no jewellery on hands, and nobody works on production while sick with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
**Pest control:** screened windows, no food left out overnight, sealed containers, and a fumigation certificate from a pest control operator. Never spray insecticide near open product or packaging.
**Cleaning:** a written schedule: surfaces after each batch, floor daily, shelves weekly, a deep clean monthly.
**Chemicals:** cleaning chemicals stored on a separate shelf, away from ingredients, in their original labelled containers.
**Packaging:** new containers stored covered and off the floor. Do not reuse old bottles from the market.

blocks.title: Gas, heat and cleaning chemicals
blocks.text: Keep gas cylinders outside or in a ventilated spot away from the frying area, with a working regulator and hose. Keep a fire blanket or extinguisher within reach. Never mix bleach with other cleaners, because some combinations release harmful gas.
Surfaces, equipment and storage

Inspectors look closely at anything that touches the product. Work tables should be smooth and easy to wash, such as stainless steel or a sealed surface; rough wood holds dirt and moisture. Use food-grade plastic or stainless steel bowls, spoons and buckets, and keep them only for production. A pot that cooks family soup at night should not mix shea butter in the morning. Store dry raw materials in sealed containers on shelves, label each one with what it is and the date it was opened, and use the oldest stock first. For cosmetics and soaps, keep fragrance oils and colourants tightly closed, away from heat and sunlight.

Lighting matters too. A dim room hides dirt and makes it hard to see a foreign object in the product. Add a bright bulb with a cover over the main work table, so a broken bulb cannot drop glass into an open batch.
Make cleaning visible with a log

A cleaning log is a simple table on the wall: date, task, done by, checked by. One line per day. It proves to the inspector, and to you, that cleaning really happens. Keep old sheets in your compliance file. A clean room with no record looks the same as a room cleaned once for the visit.

takeaways: A designated room is used only for production and does not open to contamination.
Arrange materials to move one way from raw to finished, with waste leaving separately.
The WHO Five Keys translate directly into room layout and daily habits.
Fumigation, handwashing and a filled cleaning log are visible proof of hygiene.

activity.title: Map and fix your production room
steps: Measure your room and draw it on paper, marking doors and windows.
Draw arrows for the one-way flow from raw store to packed storage.
Mark any opening to a toilet, drain or refuse and plan how to close it.
Make a cleaning log sheet and start filling it today.
activity.evidence: A sketch of your room with flow arrows and one week of filled cleaning log.

lessons.title: Pricing compliance into every unit and planning batch capacity
objectives: List every compliance cost for one product, one-off and recurring
Spread compliance costs over the units you will sell during the certificate's life
Plan batch sizes and production days that meet a buyer's monthly order
Check that the final unit price still leaves profit

blocks.text: Compliance is a real cost of production, like oil or packaging. If you do not build it into your price, it quietly eats your profit. The good news is that, once spread over hundreds of units, it usually adds only a small amount to each pack. This lesson shows you how to calculate it and how to plan capacity once bigger buyers start ordering.

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.caption: Compliance costs belong in your costing sheet like any other input.

blocks.text: Step 1: list your compliance costs

Separate costs that happen once per certificate from those that recur. For the NAFDAC fee, use the payment advice you receive. When this course was written, NAFDAC's MSME page showed the micro scale fee as ₦36,737.50 for food and ₦41,000 for cosmetics; fees can change, so always confirm on the page or advice. Other costs, such as medical tests or fumigation, vary by city and provider, so get quotes.

head: Cost item
Type
Example amount (approximate)
rows: ₦36,737.50 as shown on NAFDAC's MSME page
Room improvements: mesh, paint, handwash point

blocks.text: Step 2: spread the cost over units

blocks.title: Worked example: compliance cost per pack of chin-chin
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Jos uses the figures in the table above for her chin-chin. She sells about 300 packs a month and her micro scale listing lasts two years.
steps: She plans to repeat fumigation and medical tests once in the second year as well, adding 25,000 + 45,000 = ₦70,000. Two-year total: ₦276,737.50.
Units sold over two years: 300 packs a month times 24 months = 7,200 packs.
Compliance cost per pack: 276,737.50 divided by 7,200 = about ₦38.44, which she rounds up to ₦40.
Her other costs per pack (ingredients, gas, packaging, labour) come to ₦620. Total cost is now ₦660.
blocks.result: At her selling price of ₦1,000, profit per pack is ₦340. Compliance takes ₦40 of each pack, which is affordable, and it unlocks supermarket sales she could not reach before.

blocks.title: If volume is low
blocks.text: If Grace sold only 50 packs a month, the same costs over 1,200 packs would be about ₦231 per pack. Low volume makes compliance expensive per unit, which is why the products you list first should be your best sellers.

blocks.title: Same costs, different volumes
items: 300 packs a month
50 packs a month
blocks.caption: Volume decides how heavy compliance feels in each unit.

blocks.text: Step 3: plan capacity for a bigger buyer

Once you have a number, a supermarket may ask for a fixed monthly quantity. Before you agree, check that your approved room and process can make it without cutting corners. Work in batches, because your batch record and batch number are tied to each one.

items: Write your batch size from the master formula, for example 60 packs per batch.
Write how many batches you can make safely in one production day, including cleaning between batches, for example 2.
Work out daily output: 60 times 2 = 120 packs.
Divide the monthly demand by daily output. For 300 existing packs plus a new 200-pack order, 500 divided by 120 is about 4.2, so 5 production days a month.
Check raw materials, packaging and cash for 5 days of production before you say yes.

blocks.text: Step 4: protect your cash between batches

Supermarkets and distributors often pay some weeks after delivery, while you pay for ingredients, packaging and gas before you produce. Ask each buyer for their payment terms in writing before the first delivery. Then work out how many weeks of production you must fund before the first payment arrives. For example, if one month of production for a new 200-pack order costs about ₦124,000 (200 packs at ₦620) and the buyer pays 30 days after delivery, you need at least that amount set aside, plus a cushion, before you accept. Do not take money meant for the next listing renewal or fumigation to fund a big order; keep a separate small savings pot for compliance so those dates are always covered.
Review your compliance cost per unit once a year. If sales grow, the cost per unit falls and you may be able to hold your price while competitors raise theirs.

If the numbers do not fit, say so and agree a smaller starting quantity. A buyer forgives a modest first order far more easily than a missed delivery or a batch made in a rush that fails quality checks.

takeaways: Separate one-off and recurring compliance costs, and confirm current fees with NAFDAC.
Compliance cost per unit equals total cost over the certificate's life divided by units sold in that time.
Low volume makes compliance expensive per unit, so list best sellers first.
Plan orders in batches and production days your approved room can handle safely.

activity.title: Cost your compliance
steps: List every compliance cost for your lead product and mark it once or recurring.
Get at least one real quote for medical tests and fumigation in your city.
Calculate compliance cost per unit over two years.
Add it to your unit cost and check your profit at your current price.
activity.evidence: A costing sheet showing compliance cost per unit and the updated profit per unit.

quiz.q: Chiamaka needs approval by early October. Using ninety working days plus two weeks of buffer, roughly how many weeks should she allow?
quiz.explain: 90 working days divided by 5 is 18 weeks, plus 2 weeks of buffer gives 20 weeks.

quiz.q: When is the best time to book the facility inspection?
options: On a day the room is empty so it looks tidy
On a production day after fumigation and medical tests are done
quiz.explain: The inspector should see your real process, and your certificates should already be in hand.

quiz.q: Grace's back door opens toward the compound toilet. What is the best fix?
options: Seal that door and use only the door to the corridor
Keep the door open for ventilation
Move the packing table near that door
quiz.explain: The production room must not open directly to a source of contamination, so that opening must be closed.

quiz.q: Total compliance costs over two years are ₦180,000 and she expects to sell 6,000 units in that time. What is the compliance cost per unit?
quiz.explain: 180,000 divided by 6,000 is 30, so ₦30 per unit.

quiz.q: Which habit best matches the WHO key 'Separate raw and cooked'?
options: Washing hands only at the end of the day
Using separate tables and utensils for raw materials and finished goods
quiz.explain: Separation means raw and finished items never share surfaces, tools or storage.

quiz.q: She makes 80 units per batch and 2 batches per day. A buyer wants 640 units a month. How many production days does she need?
quiz.explain: Daily output is 80 times 2 = 160. 640 divided by 160 is 4 days.

modules.title: Growth: Standards, Traceability and Staying Approved
modules.overview: Approval is the start, not the finish. This module covers SON's MANCAP certification for products outside NAFDAC's scope, the batch records and recall plan that protect you as you grow, and the renewal calendar and 90-day plan that keep your products legally on the shelf.

lessons.title: Selling wider: SON MANCAP, Nigerian Industrial Standards and buyer requirements
objectives: Explain what MANCAP is and which sectors SON lists under it
List the documents and steps SON gives for MANCAP certification
Prepare a supplier pack for a supermarket or distributor
Decide whether NAFDAC, SON or both apply by checking with the right office

blocks.text: Not every maker sells food or cosmetics. Women in Nigeria also produce adire and other textiles, leather bags and sandals, candles, simple electrical items, building materials such as paving stones and blocks, and more. For many locally manufactured products, the body that matters is the **Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON)**, through its **Mandatory Conformity Assessment Programme (MANCAP)**.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.alt: A person standing beside a large certificate with a seal
blocks.caption: MANCAP certification shows a buyer your product meets a Nigerian Industrial Standard.

blocks.text: What MANCAP is

SON describes MANCAP as a product certification scheme for locally manufactured products in Nigeria, set up in 2006, to check that products comply with the relevant **Nigerian Industrial Standards (NIS)** before they are sold or exported. SON's service page lists six sectors: textiles and leather products; electrical and electronics; chemical products; mechanical products; civil, building and mining; and food products.

blocks.title: NAFDAC and SON: ask, do not assume
blocks.text: Food, drinks and cosmetics sold to the public need NAFDAC approval. SON's MANCAP sector list also includes food and chemical products, so for some products both bodies may have a role. Before you spend money, ask your nearest SON state office whether your product has an NIS and needs MANCAP, and keep their answer in writing.
MANCAP steps, from SON's own FAQ

items: Contact your nearest SON state office for the application form and guidance, or apply on the MANCAP platform (mancap.son.gov.ng).

Submit your CAC certificate, an on-the-spot test report from a SON laboratory or a laboratory accredited by the Institute of Public Analysts of Nigeria (IPAN), and proof of payment for the form and certification.
Prepare for factory inspections. SON states that at least two quarterly inspections take place before certification.
Receive the MANCAP certificate and the MANCAP logo, which carries a unique identification number. SON gives 60 days from receipt of a complete application.
Expect continued quarterly inspections while the certificate is valid. It is valid for three years, after which you recertify.

blocks.text: SON's FAQ also mentions a **six-month fast track verification** for MSMEs, which lets a small producer trade while working towards full certification, and states that MANCAP-certified products can be exported to West African countries. Fees vary, so SON directs applicants to its state offices for current charges.

blocks.title: The MANCAP cycle
items: Apply with test report
Two quarterly inspections
Certificate and logo
Quarterly surveillance
Recertify after three years
blocks.caption: MANCAP is a three-year cycle with inspections throughout, not a one-time stamp.

blocks.title: Worked example: adire for a retail chain
blocks.context: For example, Bola in Abeokuta dyes adire fabric with four workers. A retail chain wants to stock her fabric, and a trader wants to take some to Accra.
steps: Bola visits the SON state office and asks whether her fabric falls under a Nigerian Industrial Standard and needs MANCAP. She writes down the officer's name and answer.
She is told which tests apply, for example colour fastness, and arranges an on-the-spot test report at a SON or IPAN-accredited laboratory.
She plans for two quarterly inspections before certification, so she expects at least six months from her first inspection, and asks about the MSME fast track.
She builds a three-year calendar: certificate date, then a reminder every three months for surveillance inspections, and a recertification reminder six months before the third anniversary.
blocks.result: Bola knows her timeline before promising dates to the retail chain, and MANCAP certification will also support her export sales within West Africa.

blocks.text: Getting ready for SON's inspections

The habits from Module 2 carry over. SON inspectors want to see that you make the product the same way every time and can show it. Write down your raw material specifications (for example fabric type and dye brand for adire, or cement grade and mix ratio for paving stones), keep records of each production run, and keep your test reports filed by date. Because surveillance continues every quarter for three years, the records must stay alive, not be prepared once for the first visit. Use the MANCAP logo only on products and pack sizes covered by your certificate, since its unique number links the mark to your factory.
What bigger buyers usually ask for

head: Item
Why the buyer asks
Where it comes from
rows: To sell a regulated or standard-covered product legally
Many supermarkets scan items at the till
GS1 Nigeria, the official barcode numbering body
To set shelf prices and margins
To rotate stock and handle complaints

blocks.title: Barcodes from unofficial sellers
blocks.text: Some online sellers offer cheap barcodes. If a supermarket's system needs numbers registered to your company, a resold code may not work. Ask the buyer what they accept and get numbers from GS1 Nigeria if required.

takeaways: MANCAP is SON's certification scheme for locally manufactured products against Nigerian Industrial Standards.
SON asks for a CAC certificate, a test report from a SON or IPAN-accredited lab and payment, then inspects at least twice before certifying.
A MANCAP certificate is valid for three years, with quarterly surveillance.
Supermarkets usually want registration, regulatory approval, barcodes and batch information.

activity.title: Build your buyer pack
steps: Write down whether your product falls under NAFDAC, SON or both, and who confirmed it.
List the documents a supermarket or distributor would ask you for.
Mark each one: have it, in progress, or not started.
Ask one target buyer what they require for new suppliers and add anything missing.
activity.evidence: A buyer pack checklist with the status of each item and your regulator confirmation note.

lessons.title: Batch records, traceability and recalls: training your team to keep them
objectives: Design a batch numbering system that links every pack to its production record
Fill in a batch manufacturing record and a distribution record
Handle a customer complaint and run a recall step by step
Train a new worker on records using a show, do, check method

blocks.text: As you grow, products leave your hands and travel to shops and homes you never see. **Traceability** means that from any one pack, you can find out when it was made, from which raw materials, by whom, and where the rest of that batch went. It is what lets you deal with a problem in one batch without losing your whole business.

blocks.name: clipboard
blocks.alt: A clipboard with a record sheet
blocks.caption: Every batch gets a record, and every record can be traced to the packs on shelves.

blocks.text: A batch number that means something

A batch is everything made from one mix under the same conditions. Give each batch a unique code and print it on every pack from that batch. A simple pattern: **product code, date, batch of the day**. For example, CC-260312-02 means chin-chin, made on 12 March 2026, second batch that day. Anyone in your team can read it, and it never repeats.
The batch manufacturing record

head: Section
What to record
rows: Product, batch number, date, batch size, made by, checked by
Each ingredient, quantity used, supplier, supplier's batch or receipt date, expiry date
Key times and temperatures, for example oil temperature and frying time; any problems
Units packed, units rejected and why
Number of packs kept and where stored
Signature of the person who checked the batch before sale

blocks.text: Then keep a **distribution record**: date, buyer name and phone, batch number and quantity. A notebook works; a simple spreadsheet works better because you can search it. Keep retained samples from each batch until after its best-before date, so you can compare them with a complained-about pack.

blocks.title: Tracing one pack
items: Pack batch code
Batch manufacturing record
Raw material suppliers
Distribution record
Every buyer of that batch
blocks.caption: One code on the pack opens the whole history of that batch.

blocks.text: How long to keep records

Keep each batch record, distribution record and retained sample at least until the batch's best-before date has passed, and keep the paper or digital records for longer, ideally for the life of your certificate, because an inspector may ask to see past batches. Store paper records in a dry box away from the production floor, and photograph each completed sheet into a dated phone folder as a backup. If water, termites or a lost phone destroy one copy, the other survives.
When a customer complains

blocks.title: Worked example: a complaint and a quiet recall
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt makes chin-chin. A shop owner calls to say a customer found a pack that smells rancid. The pack code is CC-260312-02.
steps: Ngozi logs the complaint: date, caller, shop, pack code, problem. She asks the shop to keep the pack.
She immediately stops selling CC-260312-02 and sets aside any unsold packs from it in her store.
She opens the retained sample of that batch. It also smells slightly off. The batch record shows the frying oil was from a new supplier, bought cheaper.
Her distribution record shows the batch was 120 packs: 40 to this shop, 50 to a supermarket, 30 sold directly on WhatsApp to 9 customers.
She calls both shops to remove the batch, replaces it with packs from batch CC-260314-01, and messages the 9 WhatsApp customers offering a replacement.
She returns to her previous oil supplier, records the cause and the action taken, and reports the issue to NAFDAC through its complaints line, as her approved product was affected.
blocks.result: Within two days every remaining pack from the batch is off the shelves, customers are looked after, and the cause is fixed. Without batch and distribution records, she would have had to pull every pack she had sold.

blocks.title: When it could hurt someone, act first
blocks.text: If a complaint suggests illness, a foreign object or an allergic reaction, stop sales of that batch at once, keep the evidence, encourage the affected person to see a health worker, and contact NAFDAC. Do not wait to be sure before you stop sales.
Training a worker on records: show, do, check

items: **Show:** fill one batch record yourself while the worker watches, explaining each line and why it matters.
**Do:** the worker fills the next batch record while you watch, and you correct gently on the spot.
**Check:** for the next five batches, the worker fills the record alone and you check and sign each one.
When five records in a row are complete and correct, check weekly instead, and keep the trained worker's name on your role sheet.

blocks.text: Explain the why, not only the how. A worker who understands that the batch code is what saves the business in a recall will not skip it on a busy Saturday.

takeaways: A batch code such as product-date-number links every pack to its record.
Batch, distribution and complaint records together make a recall small and quick.
Keep retained samples until after the best-before date.
Stop sales of a batch first when safety is in doubt, then investigate.
Train workers with show, do, check, and sign off records until they are reliable.

activity.title: Set up traceability
steps: Create product codes and a batch numbering pattern for your products.
Make a batch manufacturing record template using the table in this lesson.
Make a distribution record and a complaint log.
Fill all three for your next real batch.
activity.evidence: One completed batch record, distribution record and complaint log template for a real batch.

lessons.title: Staying approved: renewals, label changes and your 90-day product compliance plan
objectives: Build a product compliance calendar with every expiry and recurring check
Recognise changes that need regulator approval before you make them
Decide when to move from micro scale to small scale
Write a dated 90-day plan with clear actions

blocks.text: The most common way approved makers fall out of compliance is not fraud. It is forgetting: a listing certificate that expires while stock is still selling, a fumigation certificate that went out of date, a new worker who never did the medical tests. A calendar fixes most of this.

blocks.name: spiral-calendar-pad
blocks.caption: Every certificate in your file has a date, and every date belongs in your calendar.

blocks.text: What goes on your product compliance calendar

head: Item
Validity or frequency
Reminder
rows: Two years, as stated by NAFDAC
Each quarter, and six months before expiry
As your inspector or pest control operator advises
As NAFDAC or your inspector requires, and for every new worker
At hiring, and on the due date

blocks.title: Before any change, ask NAFDAC or SON
items: New ingredient or supplier grade
New pack size or material
New claim on the label
New production address
New product or flavour
blocks.caption: Each of these can mean the approved product or premises is no longer what was assessed.

blocks.text: Changes are part of growth, but they need care. If you change the formula, the premises, the label claims or add a product, contact NAFDAC (or SON) and ask what is required **before** the changed product goes on sale. Update your master formula, label artwork and compliance file at the same time, so the paperwork always matches the product.

blocks.title: Worked example: working out reminder dates
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Kano collected her micro scale listing certificate on 10 February 2026. Her fumigation was done on 5 January 2026 and her pest control operator advised repeating it every six months.
steps: Listing expiry: two years after 10 February 2026 is 10 February 2028.
Renewal reminder: six months before expiry is 10 August 2027. She enters it with an alarm.
Fumigation: six months after 5 January 2026 is 5 July 2026, then 5 January 2027, and so on. She sets a reminder one month before each, on 5 June and 5 December.
Compliance day: she sets a repeating event on the first Monday of every month.
blocks.result: Zainab's phone now warns her early for every date, so her renewal starts six months before stock would become illegal to sell.

blocks.text: When to move up to small scale

items: You need to list a sixth product, beyond the five allowed at micro scale.
Your production staff will go above the five-employee micro scale description.
Buyers want larger volumes than your single designated room can make safely.
You are ready to write SOPs and pay for water analysis and certificates of analysis.

blocks.title: Worked example: a two-product launch plan in 90 days
blocks.context: For example, Esi in Calabar makes whipped shea butter and black soap. She has a CAC certificate, a draft label and a spare room, but has not applied to NAFDAC. Today is 1 November.
steps: Days 1 to 14 (by 14 November): write the master formula for both products, seal retained samples, fix the label using the field checklist.
Days 15 to 30 (by 30 November): screen the window, paint, set up handwashing, start the cleaning log, book fumigation and staff medical tests.
Days 31 to 45 (by 15 December): create the portal account, upload documents, pay through Remita against the payment advice, book the inspection for a production day in early January.
Days 46 to 90 (by 30 January): set up batch, distribution and complaint records, run her first inspection, answer any queries with proof, and contact two target shops with her buyer pack.
She puts the expected certificate date, about eighteen weeks after applying, plus two weeks of buffer, in her calendar, and plans her label print run for after that date.
blocks.result: Esi has a dated plan with four checkpoints, every task tied to something she learned in this course, and a realistic idea of when she can sell to shops legally.

blocks.title: Keep the plan where you see it
blocks.text: Put the 90-day plan on the production room wall next to the cleaning log, and tick tasks as you finish them. Review it on your monthly compliance day and move any slipped task to a new date rather than deleting it.

Your compliance file is now an asset. It holds your route decision, master formulas, labels, certificates, batch records and calendar. A bank, grant programme or large buyer who sees an organised file sees a producer they can trust.

takeaways: Most lapses come from forgotten expiry dates, so put every date in a calendar with early reminders.
Ask the regulator before changing the formula, pack, claims, premises or product range.
Move to small scale when you need more products, more staff or more capacity.
A 90-day plan works best with dated checkpoints and a monthly review.

activity.title: Write your calendar and 90-day plan
steps: List every certificate and recurring check you have or will need, with dates.
Enter each one in your phone calendar with the reminders in this lesson.
Write a 90-day plan in four blocks with dated actions.
Set your monthly compliance review day.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your compliance calendar and your written 90-day plan.

quiz.q: Which documents does SON's MANCAP FAQ list for an application?
options: A NAFDAC number and a barcode
CAC certificate, a test report from a SON or IPAN-accredited lab, and proof of payment
quiz.explain: SON lists the CAC certificate, an on-the-spot test report from a SON or IPAN-accredited laboratory, and proof of payment.

quiz.q: A MANCAP certificate was issued on 1 March 2026. When does SON's stated validity end?
quiz.explain: SON states MANCAP certificates are valid for three years, with quarterly surveillance during that time.

quiz.q: What does the batch code SB-260415-01 most likely tell Ngozi's team?
options: Product SB, made on 15 April 2026, first batch that day
quiz.explain: The pattern is product code, date (year, month, day) and batch of the day.

quiz.q: A customer reports feeling ill after eating from batch CC-260312-02. What should happen first?
options: Wait for more complaints to be sure
Stop selling that batch, keep the evidence, and contact NAFDAC
Relabel the batch with a new date
Offer a discount on the batch
quiz.explain: When safety is in doubt, stop sales first, keep evidence and report, then investigate.

quiz.q: A batch of 150 packs went 60 to Shop A, 50 to Shop B and the rest to WhatsApp customers. How many packs went to WhatsApp customers?
Esi wants to add a sixth product to her micro scale listing. What does this signal?
options: She can add it using an existing number
It is time to consider moving to small scale
She should stop making one product forever
quiz.explain: Micro scale allows not more than five products, so a sixth is a reason to consider the small scale route.

finalQuiz.q: Which product cannot use NAFDAC's micro scale route, according to its MSME page?
finalQuiz.explain: Fish and fish products, except dried, are excluded under micro scale, as are meat and dairy.

finalQuiz.q: What does NAFDAC issue at micro scale, and for how long is it valid?
options: A listing certificate valid for two years
finalQuiz.explain: NAFDAC's MSME page states the listing certificate is valid for two years.

finalQuiz.q: Which item is part of the MSME document list?
options: One vetting sample and three labels
finalQuiz.explain: The procedure asks for one vetting sample and three labels, among other documents.

finalQuiz.q: A batch of 3,000 g uses 2,250 g shea butter. What percentage of the batch is shea butter?
Which medical tests does NAFDAC list for food handlers' fitness certificates?
options: Sputum, stool, urine, Widal and Hepatitis B
finalQuiz.explain: The MSME procedure lists sputum, stool, urinary, Widal and Hepatitis B tests.

finalQuiz.q: Approval is needed by mid-September. Allowing about 20 weeks, roughly when should she apply?
finalQuiz.explain: Twenty weeks before mid-September is about late April or early May.

finalQuiz.q: Which room arrangement best supports one-way flow?
options: Raw materials stored under the packing table
Packing table next to the waste bin
Raw store, preparation, processing, cooling, then packing, in that order
Finished goods passed back through the mixing area
finalQuiz.explain: Materials should move in one direction so finished product never meets raw materials or waste.

finalQuiz.q: Two-year compliance costs are ₦240,000 and she sells 400 units a month. What is the compliance cost per unit?
finalQuiz.explain: 400 times 24 is 9,600 units. 240,000 divided by 9,600 is ₦25.

finalQuiz.q: How long does SON say MANCAP certification takes from receipt of a complete application?
finalQuiz.explain: SON's FAQ gives 60 days from receipt of the application when all requirements are met.

finalQuiz.q: Why keep a distribution record for each batch?
options: To find every buyer of a batch quickly if there is a recall
Because NAFDAC prints it on the label
finalQuiz.explain: Linking batch numbers to buyers lets you pull one batch from the market instead of everything.

finalQuiz.q: She wants to switch to a cheaper preservative after approval. What should she do first?
options: Print a new batch number only
Ask NAFDAC what is required before selling the changed product
Switch quietly, the label is the same
finalQuiz.explain: A formula change means the product on sale is no longer the one assessed, so ask the regulator first.

finalQuiz.q: Someone offers to arrange a NAFDAC number in one week with no inspection. What is the best sign this is not genuine?
options: Genuine registration includes facility inspection and laboratory analysis
finalQuiz.explain: NAFDAC's procedure includes inspection and lab testing, with a stated timeline of ninety working days.

capstone.title: Product Compliance Roadmap
capstone.brief: Produce a complete compliance roadmap for one of your own products: a justified comparison of the approval routes open to it, a batch and cost record template, and a compliance calendar with a 90-day plan to reach or keep approval.
steps: Compare the routes for your product (NAFDAC micro scale, small scale or regular registration, and SON MANCAP if relevant) and justify your choice in half a page.
Write the master formula with percentages and a draft label that includes every required field.
Draw your production room with one-way flow and list the fixes needed to pass inspection.
Build a record template covering batch manufacture, distribution, complaints and compliance cost per unit, and fill it for one real batch.
Create a compliance calendar with every certificate, expiry and recurring check, and write a dated 90-day plan.
evidence: Route comparison with a clear, justified choice
Master formula and label draft with all fields
Filled batch, distribution and costing record for one batch
Compliance calendar screenshot and dated 90-day plan
